1. Both the parties are aggrieved by the order passed by the learned Presiding Officer, District
Tribunal, Ranchi, in Reference Case No.05 of 1997 and have filed the instant writ petitions.
2. The parties shall be referred to as the "Management" and the "Workman-Union" hereinafter.

The Workman-Union claimed that its workmen had been working permanent and continuous nature of job in the Canteen run by the Management for the benefits of its employees working in the Bokaro Steel Plant.

All the concerned workmen were working in the Canteen under the direct control and supervision of the Management since long but the Management illegally and arbitrary terminated their services with effect from 29.07.1979.

The Workman-Union challenged the illegal termination of services of the concerned workmen which was first referred before the Labour Court,
Bokaro Steel City and numbered as Reference Case No.04 of 1990.
The Workman-Union thereafter filed a petition for impleading the Bokaro Steel Plant as a necessary party in the Labour Court to the Reference and it was thereafter the Management was impleaded.

13. As regards the workmen, it is stated that the Workman-Union has filed the instant writ petition,
i.e. W.P. (L) No.3585 of 2009, seeking a direction to the Management to reinstate the concerned workmen with full back-wages with effect from 29.07.1979 as per the award dated 25.08.2008 (pronounced on 13.10.2008) which actually is the relief granted by the learned Labour Court and this Court really fails to Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 understand how such writ petition seeking enforcement of the award is maintainable.
14. Accordingly, W.P. (L) No.3585 of 2009 is ordered to be dismissed as not maintainable.

15. Adverting to W.P. (L) No.1716 of 2009, the same has been filed by the Management for the grant of the following reliefs:-
"For the issuance of an appropriate writ/writs, order/orders, direction/directions or a writ in the nature of Certiorari for quashing of the award dated 25th August, 2008 passed by the Learned Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal, Ranchi passed in Reference Case No. 5 of 1997 whereby and whereunder reference has been answered positively in favour of the work workman by holding the termination of 128 workman who are contract workers as not proper and justified and has been directed to be reinstated with full backwages w.e.f. 29.7.79."

At the outset, it needs to be reiterated herein that while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence unless the authority has exceeded the jurisdiction or acted perversely.
Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 18.

It is amply settled that High Court can set aside or ignore the findings of fact of an appropriate court if there is no evidence to justify such conclusion and if no reasonable person could possibly have come to the conclusion which the courts below have come or in other words, appointment which was perverse in law.

19. It also needs to be mentioned herein that the burden of proof of employer-employee relationship lies on the person asserting and such a relationship must be established through concrete evidence on record as it is a question of fact determined by the cumulative effect of all material placed before the adjudicatory forum.
20.

It is a trite that burden to prove that a claimant was in the employment of a particular management, primarily lies on the person who claims to be so but the degree of proof, so required,
varies from case to case.

It is neither feasible nor advisable to lay down an abstract rule to determine Bokaro Steel Plant vs Their Workman Represented By Bokaro ... on 30 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117549785/

It is essentially a question of fact to be determined by having regard to the cumulative effect of the entire material placed before the adjudicatory forum by the claimant and the management.

21. Where the plea of the workman that he was employee of the company is denied by the company,
then it is not for the company to prove that he was not an employee.

The burden of proof being on the workmen to establish the employer-employee relationship an adverse inference cannot be drawn against the employer that if he were to Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 produce books of accounts they would have proved
employer-employee relationship

The question whether the relationship between the parties is one of employer and employee is a pure question of fact and ordinarily, the High Court while exercising its power of judicial review cannot interfere therewith unless such finding is manifestly or obviously erroneous or perverse.

23. The appointment of a workman can be proved by producing the appointment letter, written agreement, attendance register, salary register, leave records, deposit of PF contribution, ESI etc. by the workman.
The workman can also call for the record from the Management.
Mere some self-statements (like affidavits) are not sufficient without concrete evidence.

24. Now, in case the findings recorded by the Tribunal are analyzed bearing in mind the aforesaid exposition of law, this Court has no hesitation to conclude that the findings recorded by the Tribunal are totally perverse.

However, before adverting to the findings, it needs to be observed that the Management is under obligation to give certain facilities to its employees under the Factories Act and various other enactments so also to ensure social security and welfare of its employees and their families which are inherent activities of the Steel Plant as an employer.

25. The issue involved in the instant lis has been time & again raised before the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of canteens run by steel plants Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 and the matter has been dealt with in detail by Hon'ble Three Judges of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Balwant Rai Saluja and Another v. Air India Limited and Others, (2014) 9 SCC 407, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that workers, to be called the employees of the factory for all purposes,
they would need to satisfy the test of employer-employee relationship and it must be shown that the employer exercises absolute and effective control over the said workers.

Now, in cases the tests are applied to the instant case, it would be noticed that the workmen in this case were appointed by the contractors which cannot treated as appointments made by the Management.
28. There first test of "who appoints the workers?" fails in the present case.
29. The second test of "who pays the salary/remuneration?" also fails as no salary is paid to the workers by the Management and what is paid is by the contractors.

30. The third test of "who has the authority to dismiss?" again fails in the present case as there is nothing on record to indicate that it was the Management that took a decision about discontinuation of any individual of the workmen, rather the contractors have terminated them.

31. The fourth test of "who can take disciplinary action?" also fails in the present case as there is no question of taking any disciplinary action by the Management against the workmen who were treated as the employees of the contractors.
32. The fifth test as to "whether there is continuity of service?"
again does not get fulfilled in the instant case as it is not the case where same employees are continued through different contractors and that the contractor of each individual was distinct.

The sixth test as prescribed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Balwant Rai Saluja's case (supra) is not fulfilled in the instant case.

34. Apart from above, it needs to be noted that the primary work being executed by the Management is manufacturing steel and not running of canteen and, therefore, the findings arrived at by the Tribunal claiming the Contract Labour Agreement as sham and nominal and rather a camouflage are not at all sustainable and are rather perverse.

This is particularly when these findings are so rendered mainly on the basis of the provisions contained in Section 46 of the Bihar Factories Act as is evident from paragraph 73 of the Award which reads as under:-
"73.

From these discussions made above of the legal positions as advanced by to the parties this Tribunal is of the opinion that when the contract is found to be sham and nominal rather a camouflage and is run under the mandatory provision of Section 46 of the Bihar Factories Act, the workers of the canteen will be the workers of principal employer.
Now in this case the Tribunal wants to examine whether the 13 contractors notified in the notification were name lenders and the contract was a sham and camouflage?
This Tribunal finds that the management in order to prove that these 13 contractors were genuine and not sham filed and exhibited tow agreements which are Ext.M-8 and Ext.M-8/1.

The management also filed a Photostat copy of lease agreement dated 6.5.78 which could not be exhibited due Neutral Citation No.
2025:JHHC:32586 to some technical defects but the same is marked 'X' for identification.

This Tribunal after careful study of Exts.M-8, M-8/1 & 'X' is of the view that these documents are not relevant as well as not helpful to the management because they are neither registered agreement nor relating to the period and the contractors in dispute.

The learned Advocate Shri D. Mukherjee for the workers argued that Exts. M-1, M- 2, M-3 & M-4 might have been manufactured for this reference case by the company very easily because neither the workers nor their union got an opportunity to put signature on these documents.

The learned Advocate Shri Mukherjee further submitted that so far Ext.M-5 was concerned, it relates to the year 1995 whereas the dispute is of the year 1979 and as such it is a futile attempt of the management to prove the genuineness of the contractors.
Similar is the case of Ext.M-6 which is of the year 1994."

35. It also needs to be noticed that the learned Tribunal has wrongly discarded from consideration the copies of the lease agreement (Mark "X") which could not be exhibited due to some technical defect as is evident from the observations made in paragraph 73 (supra) and further, keeping out of consideration two sample agreements (Exhibit M-8 and Exhibit M-8/1) mainly on the ground that they were not registered agreements nor related to the period and did not pertain to the contract in dispute.

It shall be apt to reproduce the relevant observations as contained in paragraphs 16, 17, 28,
29, 30, 41, 76 and 90 which read as under:-
"16. Section 46 of the 1948 Act statutorily places an obligation on the occupier of a factory to provide and maintain a canteen in the factory where more than two hundred and fifty workers are employed.
There is nothing in the said provision which provides for the mode in which the factory must set up a canteen.

It appears to be left to the discretion of the factory concerned to either discharge the said obligation of setting up a canteen either by way of direct involvement or through a contractor or any other third party.
By virtue of Notification No. 27(12) 89-CIF/Lab/464 dated 21- 1-1991, Rules 65 to 70 of the 1950 Rules were made applicable to M/s Air India Ground Services Department.
The Rules impose obligations upon the occupier of the factory as regards providing for and maintaining the said canteen.
Rules 65 to 70 of the 1950 Rules are in furtherance of the duty prescribed on the State Bokaro Steel Plant vs Their Workman Represented By Bokaro ...

Government to run statutory canteens as per Section 46 of the 1948 Act:
17.1.

Rule 65, inter alia, provides for an official notification and approval of the occupier canteen facility as well as additional Neutral Citation No.
2025:JHHC:32586 guidelines regarding the construction, accommodation, hygiene,
ventilation, sanitation and other maintenance works.
17.2. Rule 66 prescribes for setting up a dining hall with adequate space and furniture along with reservation of dining space for women employees.

17.3. Rule 67 enumerates the requisite equipment such as utensils, furniture,
uniforms for the canteen staff and other equipment to be purchased and maintained in a hygienic manner.
17.4. Rule 68 prescribes that the prices to be charged on foodstuffs and other items will be on a non-profit basis, as approved by the Canteen Managing Committee.
17.5. Rule 69 illustrates the procedure for handling the auditing of accounts, under the supervision of the Canteen Managing Committee as well as Inspector of Factories.
17.6. Lastly, Rule 70 enumerates the consultative role of the Managing Committee regarding, inter alia, the quality and quantity of foodstuffs served, arrangement of menus, duration for meals, etc.
It also prescribes that such a committee must have equal representation of persons nominated by the occupier and elected members by the workers of the factory.
The Manager is entrusted with determining and supervising the procedure for conducting such elections and dissolving the Committee at the expiry of its two-year statutory term.

28. The 1948 Act is a social legislation and it provides for the health, safety, welfare,
working hours, leave and other benefits for workers employed in factories and it also provides for the improvement of working conditions within the factory premises.
Section 2 of the 1948 Act is the interpretation clause.

Apart from others, it provides the definition of "worker" under Section 2(l) of the 1948 Act, to mean a Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 person employed, directly or through any other agency, whether for wages or not, in any manufacturing or cleaning process.
29. Section 46 of the 1948 Act requires the establishment of canteens in factories employing more than two hundred and fifty workers.

The State Government have been given power under the section to make rules requiring that such canteens be provided in the factory under sub-section (2), the items for which rules are to be framed have been specified.
The sub-section also contemplates the delegation by the State Government the power to the Chief Inspector to make rules in respect of the food to be served in such canteens and their charges.
In exercise of the rule-making power, the Delhi State has framed and notified the 1950 Rules, in which Rules 65 to 70 are incorporated to give effect to the purpose of Section 46 of the 1948 Act.

The question before us is "when the company is admittedly required to run the canteen in compliance with the statutory obligation under Section 46 of the 1948 Act,
whether the canteen employees employed by the contractor are to be treated as the employees of the company only for the purpose of the 1948 Act or for all the other purposes."
41.

We conclude that the question as regards the status of workmen hired by a contractor to work in a statutory canteen established under the provisions of the 1948 Act has been well settled by a catena of decisions of this Court.

This Court is in agreement with the principle laid down in Indian Petrochemicals case [Indian Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. v. Shramik Sena, (1999) 6 SCC 439 : 1999 SCC (L&S)
1138] wherein it was held that: (SCC p. 449, para 22) Neutral Citation No.
2025:JHHC:32586 "22. ... the workmen of a statutory canteen would be the workmen of the establishment for the purpose of the 1948 Act only and not for all other purposes."

entities.text:

1138
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We add that the statutory obligation created under Section 46 of the 1948 Act, although establishes certain liability of the principal employer towards the workers employed in the given canteen facility, this must be restricted only to the 1948 Act and it does not govern the rights of employees with reference to appointment, seniority, promotion, dismissal, disciplinary actions, retirement benefits, etc., which are the subject-matter of various other legislations, policies, etc.
Therefore, we cannot accept the submission of Shri Jayant Bhushan, learned counsel that the employees of the statutory canteen ipso facto become the employees of the principal employer.

76. It has been noticed above that workmen hired by a contractor to work in a statutory canteen established under the provisions of the 1948 Act would be the said workmen of the given factory or corporation, but for the purpose of the 1948 Act only and not for all other purposes.
Therefore, the appellant workmen, in the present case, in light of the settled principles of law, would be workmen of Air India, but only for the purposes of the 1948 Act.
Solely by virtue of this deemed status under the 1948 Act, the said workers would not be able to claim regularisation in their employment from Air India.

As has been observed in Indian Petrochemicals case , (1999) 6 SCC 439 , the 1948 Act does not govern the rights of employees with reference to recruitment, seniority, promotion,
retirement benefits, etc.
These are governed by other statutes, rules, contracts or policies.

90. In terms of the above, the reference is answered as follows: the workers engaged by a contractor to work in the statutory canteen of a Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 factory would be the workers of the said factory, but only for the purposes of the 1948 Act, and not for other purposes,
and further for the said workers, to be called the employees of the factory for all purposes, they would need to satisfy the test of employer-employee relationship and it must be shown that the employer exercises absolute and effective control over the said workers."

40. opennyai_summary.facts:
The Workman-Union claimed that its workmen had been working permanent and continuous nature of job in the Canteen run by the Management for the benefits of its employees working in the Bokaro Steel Plant.
All the concerned workmen were working in the Canteen under the direct control and supervision of the Management since long but the Management illegally and arbitrary terminated their services with effect from 29.07.1979.
The Workman-Union challenged the illegal termination of services of the concerned workmen which was first referred before the Labour Court,
Bokaro Steel City and numbered as Reference Case No.04 of 1990.
The Management filed a review petition before the Labour Court against the order of impleadment, but the same was rejected vide order dated 27.01.1994.
The Management thereafter moved the Patna High Court (Ranchi Bench) by filing a writ petition challenging the aforesaid order of the Labour Court which was registered as C.W.J.C. No.1004 of 1994 and the High Court confirmed the order passed by the Labour Court.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
At the outset, it needs to be reiterated herein that while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence unless the authority has exceeded the jurisdiction or acted perversely.
It is amply settled that High Court can set aside or ignore the findings of fact of an appropriate court if there is no evidence to justify such conclusion and if no reasonable person could possibly have come to the conclusion which the courts below have come or in other words, appointment which was perverse in law.
19. It also needs to be mentioned herein that the burden of proof of employer-employee relationship lies on the person asserting and such a relationship must be established through concrete evidence on record as it is a question of fact determined by the cumulative effect of all material placed before the adjudicatory forum.
20.
It is a trite that burden to prove that a claimant was in the employment of a particular management, primarily lies on the person who claims to be so but the degree of proof, so required,
varies from case to case.
It is neither feasible nor advisable to lay down an abstract rule to determine Bokaro Steel Plant vs Their Workman Represented By Bokaro ... on 30 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117549785/
4
It is essentially a question of fact to be determined by having regard to the cumulative effect of the entire material placed before the adjudicatory forum by the claimant and the management.
21. Where the plea of the workman that he was employee of the company is denied by the company,
then it is not for the company to prove that he was not an employee.
The burden of proof being on the workmen to establish the employer-employee relationship an adverse inference cannot be drawn against the employer that if he were to Neutral Citation No. 2025:JHHC:32586 produce books of accounts they would have proved
The question whether the relationship between the parties is one of employer and employee is a pure question of fact and ordinarily, the High Court while exercising its power of judicial review cannot interfere therewith unless such finding is manifestly or obviously erroneous or perverse.
Mere some self-statements (like affidavits) are not sufficient without concrete evidence.
However, before adverting to the findings, it needs to be observed that the Management is under obligation to give certain facilities to its employees under the Factories Act and various other enactments so also to ensure social security and welfare of its employees and their families which are inherent activities of the Steel Plant as an employer.
The sixth test of "extent of control and supervision i.e. whether there exists complete control and supervision?" also does not get fulfilled in the present case as there is no linked evidence on record to prove that the Management had ever supervised the control of work by individual contractor.
The sixth test as prescribed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Balwant Rai Saluja's case (supra) is not fulfilled in the instant case.
34. Apart from above, it needs to be noted that the primary work being executed by the Management is manufacturing steel and not running of canteen and, therefore, the findings arrived at by the Tribunal claiming the Contract Labour Agreement as sham and nominal and rather a camouflage are not at all sustainable and are rather perverse.
39 . Thus, solely by virtue of deemed status under the Factories Act, 1948, the workers cannot claim their reinstatement or regularization in the employment with the Management.
This Court is in agreement with the principle laid down in Indian Petrochemicals case [Indian Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. v. Shramik Sena, (1999) 6 SCC 439 : 1999 SCC (L&S)
1138] wherein it was held that: (SCC p. 449, para 22) Neutral Citation No.
2025:JHHC:32586 "22. ... the workmen of a statutory canteen would be the workmen of the establishment for the purpose of the 1948 Act only and not for all other purposes."
